465.bp: When websites answer questions by pulling relevant content from web pages and feeding it to an AI system, those responses can only be as good as the retrieved content. A malicious actor can hide harmful instructions in a page's text or slip in misleading information, and the retrieval system will treat it like any other content. This creates a serious trust problem: the system might unknowingly follow hidden commands or output false information sourced from poisoned web pages.
465.wh: The challenge is that retrieval systems treat all content equally—they score and rank pages by relevance, not by whether the content is actually trustworthy or contains hidden attacks. A hostile webpage might rank highly and slip adversarial instructions through to the final answer. There's no automatic way to detect when text contains covert commands meant to hijack the system's behavior or when a page's retrieved snippet is designed to push biased conclusions.
465.ap: The paper introduces OpenRAG-Soc, a standardized testing suite that lets practitioners run realistic attack scenarios against their systems. The benchmark includes a collection of web pages (some weaponized with hidden instructions), multiple ways to retrieve relevant content, and several defensive tactics: cleaning up HTML and special characters, normalizing unusual Unicode tricks, and requiring the system to cite which page it drew information from before answering.
465.ww: By measuring attacks under controlled, reproducible conditions, teams can see exactly where their system fails—which retriever fumbles the attack, which defenses actually block it, and whether the system still gives useful answers after hardening. Quantifying the attack success rate and the ranking shifts it causes reveals whether your protective measures actually work or just slow things down.
465.po: Teams can now test their deployed systems for these two real threats (indirect prompt injection and retrieval poisoning) without building their own test harness from scratch. The benchmark reports attack success, rank changes in both sparse and dense retrievers, plus utility and latency, letting practitioners quickly identify and close security gaps before malicious content reaches users.

466.bp: As AI systems get distributed across millions of phones and IoT devices, keeping data private means each device trains locally on its own data, never sending raw information to a central server. But when devices have very different data distributions—one person's phone sees mostly one type of usage, another's sees completely different patterns—the shared model starts performing worse for some groups than others, even though the goal was to help everyone equally.
466.wh: Knowledge distillation is a technique where a strong model's wisdom is transferred to smaller models via a special training signal. But when a device applies this transfer based on its own local data, the global knowledge gets warped to match local patterns. More critically, rare classes (like unusual but important user behaviors) fade away because they're underrepresented locally—the system forgets about them when learning from the device's smaller slice of data.
466.ap: FedAKD adaptively adjusts how global knowledge is transferred to each device by first checking what kinds of data that device has. It then selectively disentangles two types of knowledge: the global model's overall understanding and the device-specific details. Instead of one transfer signal for everything, the method calibrates what knowledge matters most for that device's data gaps, especially protecting rare categories from being forgotten.
466.ww: By decoupling global knowledge from local data patterns, the system can preserve important generalizations for underrepresented groups while still letting each device learn from its local data. This asymmetric approach—giving special attention to locally rare categories—means the system doesn't accidentally amplify unfairness just by trying to transfer knowledge.
466.po: Experiments show the method reduces performance degradation in minority groups without hurting overall accuracy or making the shared model slower to update. Devices with highly skewed data distributions benefit most, maintaining better performance on all groups while still gaining the efficiency advantages of federated learning.

467.bp: When you shop on Amazon, you rate products one way. When you review on a critic site, you might judge differently—assigning scores for quality, value, delivery speed, and packaging separately, not just one overall rating. These multi-faceted judgments carry richer information about what users actually want, but most recommendation systems still flatten everything into a single score, losing crucial nuance about what matters for each person across different dimensions.
467.wh: A user might give a store a low 'overall' rating yet love the product quality and fast shipping—they're just unhappy about price. Existing methods either ignore the criterion-level ratings entirely or treat them as separate problems, failing to model that some users care deeply about certain dimensions while others prioritize speed or value. The system needs to learn that different people weight criteria differently and capture how items perform along each dimension.
467.ap: TaTriGR builds a three-sided relationship graph connecting users, items, and specific criteria (like quality or delivery). It learns a personalized weight for each user across criteria—capturing that one person values speed while another obsesses over price. The item's performance on each criterion gets embedded as an additional signal about what the item truly is. Information flows through this three-sided structure, and the final recommendation naturally satisfies principles from decision theory: the predicted scores respect hierarchy (better scores on important criteria matter more) and consistency (similar items get similar recommendations).
467.ww: By explicitly modeling these three relationships and forcing the predictions to obey formal decision-making rules, the system captures real preference structures. A user's personalized weights act like a translator: the same item profile gets interpreted differently for different users. The auxiliary objectives (Ideal Point Distillation and Lexicographic Consistency) reinforce that users do actually make trade-offs, which makes the learned representations more stable and interpretable.
467.po: The system produces recommendations that better match what users actually want across multiple dimensions simultaneously, not just a generic 'best item' score. When an e-commerce platform or review site deploys this, users get suggestions that respect their specific priorities—fast delivery for the busy person, quality for the perfectionist—improving satisfaction without abandoning the nuance of multi-criteria ratings.

468.bp: Governments usually make decisions through representatives who gather input and vote, but new digital tools are making it possible for citizens to participate directly in governance without intermediaries. These systems—where voting, proposals, and resource allocation happen transparently in decentralized networks—need better ways to model and understand how decisions actually get made when power flows directly among participants rather than through institutions.
468.wh: Traditional governance has clear structures: representatives, committees, procedures. Non-mediated governance is amorphous—anyone can propose anything, voting rules might change, and influence flows through social connections and consensus-building rather than formal positions. There's no standard way to diagram how information moves or how a decision actually emerges from distributed participation. Without clear mental models, it's hard to predict whether a governance system will scale or whether it might enable capture by coordinated actors.
468.ap: This paper presents a diagraming technique and toolset for visualizing non-mediated governance use-cases and the idea of Liquid Democracy, where participants can either vote directly on issues or delegate their vote to someone they trust. The toolset helps map how data (proposals, votes, delegations, discussions) flows through the system and eventually crystallizes into concrete government action or policy.
468.ww: By making the data flow visible and mappable, practitioners can see where bottlenecks occur, identify points where collusion might happen, and check whether minority voices can still influence outcomes. The diagrams ground abstract concepts about decentralized decision-making in concrete flows, making it possible to reason about whether a system is actually fair or just appears transparent.
468.po: Governance designers can now sketch out whether their liquid democracy or non-mediated system will work before deploying it at scale. They can test scenarios, identify failure modes, and refine rules—turning governance design from an art form into something more rigorous and auditable for the Web-native communities that might adopt these systems.

469.bp: Academic peer review is supposed to filter quality, catch errors, and push authors to improve their work. But as journals and conferences grow larger, managing thousands of reviews with wildly varying quality—some thorough and fair, others careless or biased—becomes nearly impossible. Editors can't read every review to check if it's sound, yet poor reviews can misdirect editorial decisions or discourage good research.
469.wh: Review quality isn't a single number; it involves many dimensions: does the reviewer understand the work, engage constructively, identify real flaws, avoid conflicts of interest, give actionable feedback? Manually assessing all these dimensions for thousands of reviews is impractical. Existing rubrics and checklists are rigid and don't capture nuance. Without automatic methods, serious quality problems go undetected until they cause damage—a rejection based on a weak review, or acceptance of flawed work.
469.ap: PeeriScope combines three layers: first, it extracts structured features from review text (length, citation of specifics, tone markers). Second, it uses large language models guided by explicit rubrics to assess quality along multiple dimensions, with the ability to extract reasoning. Third, it trains a supervised predictor to prioritize reviews that likely have problems. The system provides both a user interface and an API so editors can integrate it into their workflow—letting reviewers self-assess, editors triage efficiently, and platforms run large-scale audits.
469.ww: By breaking quality assessment into measurable dimensions and combining algorithmic features with LLM judgment, the system captures both mechanical patterns (does this review cite anything?) and semantic understanding (does it grasp the contribution?). The supervised layer learns which combinations of features actually predict quality problems editors care about, making it better than any single metric.
469.po: Editors can now flag mediocre reviews before decisions are finalized, helping them accept strong papers even if one reviewer missed the point, or reject papers based on multiple solid reviews rather than one weak one. Reviewers get constructive feedback on their own review quality. Researchers and journal operators can audit whether certain reviewer groups are systematically harsher or more shallow, creating a data foundation for improving the scientific process at scale.

470.bp: Web pages and documents often contain images alongside text—a product listing has photos, an article has charts. When you want to automatically extract structured information (product brand, price, materials) from these mixed documents, you need to understand both what the image shows and what the text describes. This is especially hard for new product categories or data types the system has never seen before.
470.wh: Existing extraction systems work well when trained on examples of a category (product type, entity class) they've seen before, but falter on novel unseen categories. More fundamentally, they usually ignore relationships between what appears in the image and what's described in text, treating the two modalities separately. They also struggle with hierarchical structure—understanding that 'Brand' is different from 'Model Number,' and that both belong under 'Product Identity.' When trying to handle both seen and unseen categories in one go, the learned representations for unseen items drift away from the correct decision boundary.
470.ap: HMGRL uses hyperbolic geometry (a curved mathematical space where hierarchies are naturally encoded as distances) to build representations that capture how images and text relate and how concepts relate hierarchically. The system learns to generate representations for new categories even without examples, using a variational approach to smooth the space. It explicitly models the gap between how 'seen' categories cluster and how 'unseen' categories should cluster, then balances these two regions so the system doesn't catastrophically ignore one or the other.
470.ww: Hyperbolic space lets the system encode hierarchical semantics naturally—the farther apart two concepts in hyperbolic space, the more different they are. This means the learned representations for 'Brand' and 'Logo' automatically reflect their relationship (Logo is part of Brand identity). By explicitly modeling the distribution gap, the system doesn't collapse to only generating seen categories, nor does it forget them entirely when trying to handle unseen ones. The two modalities (image and text) can be jointly understood rather than treated as separate threads.
470.po: The system can now extract structured information (entities, relationships) from mixed image-text documents for product categories or relation types it has never encountered, achieving higher accuracy on unseen categories while maintaining performance on seen ones. Real-world e-commerce sites and document processing pipelines gain the ability to handle emerging product types or ad-hoc data sources without manual retraining.

471.bp: Recommendation systems often use knowledge from one domain (what users buy on Amazon) to improve suggestions in another (restaurant recommendations). This knowledge transfer can make the target domain smarter—less data needed, faster learning. But there's a hidden cost: if the source domain's data is biased (certain groups receive worse suggestions there), that bias gets transmitted to the target domain, sometimes amplifying unfairness for already-marginalized groups.
471.wh: When a recommendation system transfers knowledge across domains, it assumes the learned patterns are universally helpful. But group-level biases rarely transfer cleanly—they interact with the target domain's own data distribution. Additionally, the benefits of cross-domain transfer don't accrue equally to all groups; some communities might gain more useful information than others, exacerbating disparities. Naive transfer blindly copies both good patterns and bad biases.
471.ap: CDFA has two defenses working in concert. First, it identifies which groups are disadvantaged in the source domain's disparities and strategically mixes in unlabeled data from the target domain to equilibrate how informative the training signal is across different groups. This counteracts the direct copy of source biases. Second, it uses information theory to measure how much benefit each group actually gains from the cross-domain knowledge and then redistributes those gains (via reweighting or augmentation) so all groups benefit fairly, not just the already-privileged.
471.ww: By making disparities explicit and measurable, the system can surgically correct them rather than ignoring or denying they exist. The information-theoretic redistribution doesn't arbitrarily flatten differences; instead, it ensures that marginal groups get proportional benefit. The use of unlabeled data is clever—it doesn't require annotating sensitive attributes, yet it rebalances the information density across groups, making the learned patterns less likely to magnify existing inequities.
471.po: Cross-domain recommendation systems can now transfer knowledge without accidentally amplifying group-level unfairness. Experiments show the framework reduces disparities significantly while even improving overall recommendation accuracy. Platforms can confidently leverage multi-domain data to improve personalization for everyone, not just well-represented groups.

472.bp: Fraud, hacking, and security threats in Web systems often manifest as unusual patterns of interaction—abnormal login sequences, sudden trading surges, sudden graph connection changes between accounts. These threats evolve constantly, making it hard for security systems to catch them without human monitoring. A system that detects these anomalies automatically and explains what looks suspicious is invaluable for maintaining system integrity.
472.wh: Anomaly detection in streaming interactions (new edges arriving constantly) needs to be both real-time—detecting problems within milliseconds of the suspicious behavior—and memory-efficient, because storing entire graphs can be prohibitively expensive. Standard anomaly detection methods struggle here: they either lag behind the stream (too slow) or require storing full graph state (too much memory). Additionally, explaining why something looks anomalous is crucial; a security team won't act on a black-box alert without understanding what pattern triggered it.
472.ap: The paper introduces Interaction Willingness, a metric capturing whether two entities should naturally interact based on their past behavior and graph structure. AnoD and AnoC are two algorithms that detect two types of anomalies: dense (suddenly many interactions between entities that rarely interact) and counter (interactions that break established patterns). Both use a compact data structure called High-Order Count-Min Sketch, which stores streaming graph information in near-zero memory while maintaining mathematical guarantees on accuracy.
472.ww: The Interaction Willingness metric grounds detection in a principled measure—how likely should this pair be interacting?—rather than ad-hoc thresholds. By using Count-Min Sketch, the system maintains constant memory per new edge; this means adding a million interactions doesn't degrade detection speed or memory, only storage needs. The interpretability comes naturally from the metric: explaining an anomaly means showing why Interaction Willingness suddenly changed.
472.po: Security teams can deploy these algorithms on live streaming graphs (social networks, trading systems, access logs) to catch fraud and intrusions in real-time with minimal overhead. The constant-time and constant-space guarantees mean the system scales to billions of interactions without slowing down or exhausting memory, and the interpretability ensures alerts lead to actual investigation rather than being dismissed as noise.

473.bp: AI agents that process long sequences—biological data, financial time-series, long documents—become prohibitively expensive to run because the AI model charges by the number of tokens (discrete pieces of text or data) it processes. In domains like genomics or molecular analysis, the raw sequences can span thousands or millions of positions. A researcher or startup can't afford to send all that through an expensive model, yet the model won't work on a blind summary either.
473.wh: The fundamental problem is that LLM pricing scales with input length, and raw biological or financial sequences are incompressible at face value—each position might matter. Yet the LLM cannot interpret raw sequences anyway; a genomic DNA string means nothing to a language model until a specialized tool extracts features. Passing raw sequence through the LLM is wasteful. Compressing too aggressively loses information. In multi-step agent workflows, irrelevant context from earlier steps balloons the token count without adding value.
473.ap: The paper introduces two layers of compression. Long-Sequence Compression (LSC) extracts meaningful representations from raw domain-specific sequences using task-specific tools (e.g., a bioinformatics tool for DNA, a feature extractor for time-series) before sending anything to the LLM. Prompt-based Gate-Guided Memory (PGM) works like a selective filter on intermediate states: at each step, it asks 'does the current prompt need this context,' and only carries forward relevant information, inspired by how gated recurrent networks selectively forget irrelevant history.
473.ww: By extracting semantically meaningful summaries instead of raw data, LSC dramatically reduces token count while preserving information the LLM can actually use. PGM prevents context creep in multi-step reasoning—each step doesn't accumulate every past observation, only relevant state. Together, they reduce redundancy without losing decision-critical information. The gate is learned based on the prompt, so the system adapts to what the current task needs.
473.po: A researcher can now affordably run multi-agent workflows on long biological sequences or time-series without paying prohibitive token costs. A team analyzing genomic data for drug discovery, for instance, can run agentic reasoning over tens of thousands of sequence positions instead of being limited to kilobases. The cost drops substantially, democratizing access to expensive LLM-based analysis for communities that can't absorb the overhead.

474.bp: Cybersecurity professionals defend against attacks using high-level security goals (keep data confidential, ensure systems are available) and low-level technical concepts (patch this buffer overflow vulnerability). But the connection between business objectives ('protect customer data') and technical fixes ('update OpenSSL') is murky. This gap means teams often can't explain why a particular vulnerability matters for their assets or which mitigations actually serve business goals, making risk prioritization ad-hoc and inefficient.
474.wh: Existing security standards and ontologies are static and read-only—NIST and ISO describe categories, but they don't adapt as new attacks and exploits emerge. The gap between operations (what threats are we actually seeing?) and compliance (what does the standard say we need?) widens constantly. Additionally, the standards use words ambiguously: 'Confidentiality' might mean different things in different contexts, and the chain from business goal to technical action gets lost in translation. No dynamic platform exists where the security community can collectively map these relationships and evolve the standards.
474.ap: This work proposes a wiki-style, agile ontology platform that models the full chain: Security Services (business goals like Confidentiality) connect to Security Mechanisms (technical solutions like encryption), which mitigate Attacks (types of threats), which exploit Vulnerabilities (software flaws), which can be deployed by Attackers (threat actors), who target Assets (data, systems). The system is aware of homonyms (words with multiple meanings in security contexts) and allows continuous community editing with validation, so the ontology evolves as new attacks emerge. The platform includes visualization and management tools.
474.ww: By making the chain explicit and editable, practitioners can trace why a specific patch matters for their business. The homonym-awareness prevents misunderstandings across teams (does 'Access Control' mean authentication or authorization?). The wiki approach lets the community dynamically extend the ontology as novel attacks emerge, rather than waiting for standards bodies to issue updates. Continuous community evaluation keeps mappings grounded in operational reality.
474.po: Security teams can now drill from a business goal ('ensure availability of critical systems') down to specific techniques and vulnerabilities to patch, with documented reasoning. Risk prioritization becomes more rigorous—teams see which vulnerabilities actually threaten their critical assets and which mitigations serve their top business objectives. Organizations can audit whether their current security posture aligns with strategic goals.

475.bp: Radiology reports—the text that doctors write describing what they see in X-rays and scans—need to be accurate and factually correct; a miswritten finding can lead to missed diagnoses. AI systems can now generate these reports automatically by looking at images, but generated reports often contradict the images or previous reports for the same patient. Retrieving and incorporating relevant prior reports should help the system stay factually consistent, but most methods fail to use that information effectively.
475.wh: Retrieving only coarse image-report pairs isn't enough—the system needs to understand fine-grained clinical details: which specific findings matter, how do reports about the same pathology relate across different patients, what's the hierarchical structure of medical reasoning (normal → abnormality → specific disease)? Standard cross-modal retrieval treats images and text as separate domains and learns shallow correspondences, missing the hierarchical semantic knowledge embedded in collections of reports. The result is generated reports that sound plausible but contradict facts visible in images or prior reports.
475.ap: MGK-RAG uses multi-granularity semantic similarities extracted from the text domain to guide what the system learns about images. Rather than learning a generic image-to-text match, it learns fine-grained clinical semantic alignment by looking at how reports relate to each other—which mentions of findings are similar, which diagnostic pathways typically co-occur, what's hierarchical (general symptom → specific finding). This guides the multimodal retriever. When generating a report, the system integrates retrieved reports' visual features into the original image understanding via cross-attention, enriching what the model knows about this specific patient's anatomy and pathology.
475.ww: By using report-to-report relationships as a bridge to understand images, the system learns clinical semantics that generic image models miss. The cross-attention mechanism ensures retrieved information is actually fused with the image features, not just treated as extra context. This multi-granularity approach captures both coarse correspondences (image type matches report type) and fine-grained details (this specific lesion matches this specific description across two reports).
475.po: Generated radiology reports are more factually accurate and clinically coherent, with fewer contradictions between the written findings and the image content. Hospitals deploying this system for report drafting assistance gain higher-quality outputs, reducing the radiologist's burden of editing inconsistencies and catching missed details. The hierarchical semantic understanding also improves key clinical metrics—the system doesn't just sound right, it actually matches what doctors observe.

476.bp: Mental health struggles, especially depression, often go undetected in people who don't seek formal help—isolation, shame, and accessibility barriers keep millions silent. Yet people share their inner lives on social media constantly, including through metaphor ('I'm drowning in darkness,' 'my anxiety is a cage'). If systems could recognize depression signals in these natural expressions, it could enable early intervention, destigmatize mental health, and provide crucial insights for therapeutic work.
476.wh: Metaphors are complex—the same image ('drowning') can mean depression for one person and overwhelm for another. Detecting depression from metaphors requires understanding both the surface image and the underlying psychological state it expresses. The problem is worsened by lacking large-scale annotated datasets of real metaphorical expressions linked to depression levels. Without such data, models trained on generic text don't capture the nuances of psychological expression. Additionally, purely predictive models that just output 'depressed or not' don't help clinicians; they need explanations grounded in what the person actually said.
476.ap: This work introduces the Depression-Related Metaphor Dataset (DRMD), pairing social media posts with depression severity levels (severe, moderate, minimal, or absent), annotations of which posts contain metaphors, and mappings of metaphorical source domains (e.g., 'drowning' comes from a water/submersion domain). The paper then fine-tunes large language models on this dataset, explicitly incorporating metaphorical features. Critically, the model generates explanations by referencing the specific metaphors it identified, making its reasoning interpretable.
476.ww: By training on metaphor-annotated data, the model learns that certain conceptual mappings (water domains, cage domains, darkness domains) correlate with depression severity. The explicit annotation of source domains teaches the model the psychological structures metaphor embeds—that 'drowning' isn't random, it maps internal psychological states to physical submersion, which clinicians recognize as a depression marker. The explanation mechanism ensures the model doesn't just score high on accuracy; it can tell a clinician why it flagged someone as at-risk, grounding the prediction in observable linguistic behavior.
476.po: Mental health platforms, crisis hotlines, or online communities can deploy this to flag users who may need support, with explanations that humanize the alert rather than making it feel algorithmic. The metaphor-focused approach adds empathy—the system recognizes the poetry of depression, not just keywords. Researchers gain a publicly available dataset for studying how metaphor encodes psychological state, and clinicians can better understand the language of mental health struggles.

477.bp: When AI systems process text, images, and sound together (video with subtitles, social media posts with images and comments), the data is usually complete—all three modalities present. But real-world Web content is messy: videos lack captions, images fail to load due to network issues, users disable video on low bandwidth, or privacy settings hide certain data. Systems trained on complete data fail when modalities are missing. Building systems robust to missing data is crucial for actually working in the real world.
477.wh: When a modality is missing, simple methods try to reconstruct it (guessing what sound a silent video should have) or treat it as a special missing token. But reconstruction often distorts what's actually there, and missing tokens don't capture the rich information a full modality would provide. More subtly, class prototypes—the learned idea of what a 'happy' or 'sad' video looks like—shift when data is incomplete, creating anchor drift: the decision boundary for classifying emotions moves depending on whether audio is present or absent. This instability makes the learned representation space unreliable.
477.ap: HiCoD (Hierarchical Consistency-Guided Prompt Distillation) learns a semantic space anchored by explicit class prototypes. It builds a modality-aware semantic graph that infers cross-modal structure even when some modalities are missing, using graph techniques to fill in the topology. It then uses dual-level anchoring: global prototypes derived from language models (abstract notions of 'happy' or 'angry') combined with local exemplars (actual videos in the training set that exemplify happiness). Multi-level distillation aligns unimodal features (audio alone, video alone), combined embeddings (audio + video), and even completed signals (inferred modalities) all toward the same anchor space.
477.ww: The dual-level anchoring prevents drift: even if audio is missing, the global prototype ('what happiness is') and the top-K examples ('these specific videos are happy') provide a stable reference. The semantic graph restores structure by predicting what cross-modal patterns should hold, avoiding expensive reconstruction. Multi-level distillation ensures that whether a sample has all modalities or just one, it gets represented in the same conceptual space, eliminating anchor drift.
477.po: Multimodal learning systems can now handle variable missing data—some videos with audio and captions, others with just video. They maintain consistent accuracy even under heavy missingness (e.g., 50% of videos missing audio), improving generalization on incomplete real-world data. Recommendation systems, emotion detection platforms, and accessibility tools benefit by handling incomplete Web content without retraining per modality pattern.

478.bp: Social networks protect user privacy by applying local differential privacy—a mathematical guarantee that individual user data (friends, activity) stays hidden from central servers. Yet even with strong privacy protections, the network can still be poisoned: an attacker can inject false data or modify records in ways that degrade the system's utility (the ability to classify users accurately, for instance). Balancing privacy and robustness to manipulation is a hard problem, and most privacy-preserving systems don't address poisoning.
478.wh: Local differential privacy works by intentionally adding noise to each user's data before it reaches the server, so the server sees only a scrambled aggregate. But this noise also makes it harder to detect attackers who slip in fake nodes or corrupted data—the noise masks both legitimate variation and adversarial anomalies. An attacker coordinating multiple poisoned accounts can make systematic changes that look like natural noise. Existing defenses assume clean data; they fail under privacy noise.
478.ap: CureNet defends against poisoned graph data in a privacy setting with four components. First, local data perturbation happens (standard privacy noise). Second, trimmed screening filters out outlier submissions that look suspicious, removing accounts that deviate too far from normal. Third, privacy-aware fake node pruning uses specialized techniques to detect and remove sophisticated adversaries even in noisy data—it doesn't just look for outliers, but for coordinated patterns of inauthentic behavior. Fourth, a utility recovery module restores graph learning performance after filtering, since removing nodes and edges degrades accuracy.
478.ww: By stacking defenses, the system raises the bar for attackers: they can't easily insert random fake nodes (screening catches obvious outliers) or coordinate subtle manipulations (fake node pruning detects coordinated inauthentic behavior). The privacy-aware approach uses the privacy noise structure itself—understanding what noise looks like lets the system distinguish it from attack patterns. The utility recovery ensures the privacy protections and the defense both benefit the system, not just security.
478.po: Social networks can now offer both strong user privacy (differential privacy guarantees) and robustness to data poisoning attacks. Experiments on real networks (Facebook, Twitch, GitHub, LastFM) show both that the attack is serious and that the defense significantly reduces its impact. Platforms gain confidence that privacy-preserving graph learning systems won't be compromised by coordinated adversaries inserting fake accounts or false relationships.

479.bp: Large AI models are built on top of tokenizers—systems that convert raw input (text, code, images, graphs) into discrete chunks the model can process. Text tokenizers are well-understood, but graph tokenizer is an unsolved problem: graphs have complex non-Euclidean structures (they're not 2D planes or 3D spaces), and their structure matters more than individual elements. A good graph tokenizer needs to capture essential patterns (trees, cycles, chains) and transfer those patterns across different kinds of graphs, enabling foundation models to learn from one graph domain and apply knowledge to another.
479.wh: Graphs live in curved, non-Euclidean spaces—geometry matters in ways that flat Euclidean spaces don't handle naturally. A tree structure in a social network is fundamentally different from a tree in a molecule, yet both are trees. Existing approaches either ignore structure (treating nodes as independent) or apply flat quantization (rounding real values to discrete buckets) that loses the hierarchical semantics geometry encodes. Cross-domain transfer of graph knowledge fails because different domains have different geometric properties—a social network's geometry differs from a citation network's.
479.ap: RGT uses Riemannian geometry (curved mathematical spaces where distance and angle respect the underlying structure) to build a unified framework. It defines a geometric vocabulary of fundamental structures (trees, cycles, sequences) that capture intrinsic graph patterns. A Riemannian quantizer converts continuous geometric representations into discrete tokens, using a Riemannian Straight-Through Estimator to make this differentiable for training. Crucially, a geometry-aligned decoder projects domain-specific tokens into a shared tangent space—a common reference frame where tokens from different geometric spaces can be compared.
479.ww: By using Riemannian geometry, the system naturally respects the non-Euclidean structure of graphs; distance in the curved space measures true structural dissimilarity. The geometric vocabulary captures what really distinguishes graphs—are there cycles, how deep are trees, how long are paths. The tangent space projection is clever: even though social networks and molecular graphs live in different geometric spaces, they can be represented in a shared flat space locally (tangent space), enabling transfer. This separates the identity of structures (trees, cycles) from the specific geometry of each domain.
479.po: Foundation models can now use a unified tokenizer for graphs across domains—social networks, molecules, knowledge graphs, citation networks—each retaining their geometric properties but becoming comparable at the token level. A model trained on social network patterns can transfer knowledge to molecular graphs, dramatically reducing the data needed in the target domain. This enables more efficient, more generalizable graph foundation models that can handle diverse structural domains.
